title: Node2Shell puts Microsoft and Node.js on Brotli patch duty
raw_text: A vulnerability in Google’s Brotli compression library could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code in applications that use an affected Brotli decoder to process compressed data. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497 , the high-severity flaw was first flagged in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The issue stems from an out-of-bounds write that can corrupt process memory, potentially leading to remote code execution (RCE), information disclosure, or denial of service (DoS). The Node.js project disclosed the vulnerability on October 21, 2026, alongside security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines. The exposure, however, extended beyond Node.js, forcing Microsoft to release out-of-band security updates for.NET on October 25 to address the same CVE in its Brotli decompression implementation. Separate research published by OpenSourceMalware identified the vulnerable decoder code in the Python packages Brotli and brotlicffi. Both packages have since received patched releases. The risk depends on whether an application uses an affected decoder to process attacker-controlled Brotli data. Remote code execution was demonstrated in a public GitHub proof-of-concept (PoC) lab and independently by cybersecurity firm Imperva, which gave the vulnerability its Node2Shell name. Services that decompress untrusted HTTP responses or request bodies are particularly exposed. Organizations must also account for runtimes and libraries bundled into containers and deployed application artefacts, the researchers noted. A bad block switch sends Brotli decoding out of bounds Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm used to reduce the size of data exchanged between applications and servers. Node2Shell originates in the decoder’s handling of an invalid block-type transition in a compressed stream. According to the GitHub PoC , the vulnerable DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() function can return an ambiguous failure value when a stream requests an invalid block switch. The decoder’s fast path fails to handle that return value properly, allowing processing to continue with an invalid internal state. The resulting out-of-bounds write can corrupt memory. The weakness combines an unchecked return value ( CWE-252 ) with an out-of-bounds write ( CWE-787 ). The PoC targets a vulnerable Node.js 24.22.0 Linux x86-64 build. Its exploit relies on a specific binary and memory layout, and execution is probabilistic, requiring retries in some cases. The repository also demonstrates that the same request fails against the patched Node.js 24.22.1. build, whose decoder rejects the invalid block switch. The flaw was discovered during security testing by OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer, who reported the flaw to the Node.js project. Node.js, Microsoft, and Python patches close the gap The Node.js project released fixes in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Administrators should upgrade to the relevant fixed release or a later security update, rebuild affected container images, and redeploy applications that bundle vulnerable runtimes. End-of-life Node.js versions should also be treated as affected and migrated to supported releases. Microsoft’s October 25 out-of-band updates address CVE-2026-111497 in .NET 8,9 and 10, as well as .NET 11 Release Candidate 3. The corresponding runtime versions are 8.0.33,9.0.22 and 10.0.14, with 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 for the preview line. Updated SDKs are also available. Applications using self-contained deployments or Native AOT must be rebuilt and redeployed where necessary, as updating a shared runtime alone will not replace a decoder already linked into an executable. Python maintainers have also released fixes for the affected packages. OpenSourceMalware identified Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 as patched releases, replacing vulnerable versions up to 1.2.0 and 1.2.0.2, respectively. Developers should update dependencies and verify that deployed environments use the fixed versions. Google also released patched versions of its Brotli library, fixing the underlying flaw in versions 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. As of publication, no exploitation of Node2Shell in the wild had been publicly reported, despite proof-of-concept code being available for days.

title: Alibaba AI model tried to send data to Beijing server, Cohere says
raw_text: An Alibaba AI model generated an unexpected command to upload data to a Beijing-region cloud storage service during a cybersecurity evaluation, rival developer Cohere said, raising concerns about the security of AI agents with access to enterprise systems. The model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, was being tested using Microsoft’s CTI-REALM cybersecurity benchmark, which tasked it with writing a rule to detect malicious file downloads followed by execution. Instead, it inspected local files and system settings before generating the unexpected command, according to Cohere’s report . The Canadian AI company said its isolated testing environment blocked the outgoing request. The model had indicated in its generated reasoning that it would not use any tools, contradicting the command it subsequently generated. The behavior occurred in fewer than one in 100,000 evaluation calls, Cohere said. When researchers repeated the same task, the model produced the requested detection rule without attempting an external connection. Cohere acknowledged that it could not determine whether the behavior was deliberate or resulted from information absorbed during training. Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Uncertainty over the model’s behavior The findings warrant further investigation but do not establish that Alibaba deliberately introduced a backdoor into the model, said Pareekh Jain , CEO of Pareekh Consulting. “The behavior could result from contaminated training data, a security vulnerability, or unintended AI agent actions,” Jain said. Charlie Dai , vice president and principal analyst at Forrester, said more evidence was needed to establish whether the model contained a deliberate backdoor. Researchers would need to examine the model’s weights and training pipeline , he said. They would also need network records and independent tests reproducing the behavior in different environments. “At this stage, the findings are concerning, but they don’t point to deliberate intent,” Dai said. Cohere, which competes with Alibaba in the enterprise AI market, published traces of the behavior and a reproduction script. In follow-up tests using partially supplied commands, Cohere said the model generated a cloud metadata address, such as 169.254.169.254, in 23% to 36% of completions under two test conditions. Cloud metadata services can provide access to temporary cloud credentials , although the tests did not establish that the model obtained any credentials. Sanchit Vir Gogia , chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the command contained a fixed test string rather than information extracted from a sensitive file. The Beijing location of the storage endpoint also does not establish who controls the destination. He noted that Cohere’s published trace did not include the corresponding command execution result or network telemetry, limiting what could be independently established about the attempted connection. “The threshold for constraining an agent is lower than the threshold for accusing its supplier,” Gogia said. Security controls for AI agents The immediate concern is preventing the systems from executing unauthorized commands. “Enterprises should treat AI agents as untrusted software, regardless of the model provider,” Jain said. He recommended blocking unauthorized outbound connections from AI environments and limiting access to sensitive files or cloud credentials. Organizations should also monitor agent activity and require approval before allowing AI systems to carry out critical operations. Dai also recommended running AI agents in sandboxed environments and using data-loss prevention tools to detect unauthorized attempts to transfer sensitive information. title: Lapsed US snooping law still running as senators object
raw_text:
US senators have demanded the release of a secret court ruling on a surveillance law that lets American authorities obtain foreign companies’ and citizens’ data without telling them – one of two key laws that can undermine data sovereignty for overseas citizens and organisations.

Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA 702) lapsed in June 2026, but data gathering can continue to March 2027 because of a 17 March court opinion that the senators said contains “serious abuses of Americans’ rights” – and which the Trump administration has still not declassified more than a month past its legal deadline.

Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California wrote to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton and attorney general Todd Blanche on 26 October. They demanded release of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court opinion and the names of officials who had withheld it, with a written response due by 6 November.

FISA 702 expired after the House of Representatives rejected a reauthorisation bill in June, with 19 Republicans joining Democrats to vote it down. Surveillance and data gathering continue because the same March opinion that found the abuses also permitted another year of activity.

The consequences reach further than Washington. Section 702 lets the US government compel a cloud provider to provide “technical assistance” to run a search with no protection for foreign citizens who are targeted by the act. That assistance could potentially arrive as compiled code in a software update that exfiltrates data, unreadable to the engineers who push it.

The second law is the US Cloud Act, passed in 2018 after Microsoft refused to hand over customer data held in an Irish datacentre. It compels US companies to provide data in their “possession, custody, or control” even where it sits overseas, and lets US courts attach a non-disclosure order that stops the provider from telling the data subject their data has been shared.

Together the two laws open several routes into overseas data:

  • Follow-the-sun support terms route data and metadata to global hubs, and the metadata alone can be enough for a Section 702 investigation.
  • US-authored software updates can carry “technical assistance” as compiled code that UK staff cannot inspect.
  • Data must be decrypted to be processed, so it can be scraped from memory mid-compute.
  • Even confidential computing breaks: side-channel attacks can listen to the CPU and measure power draw or timing fluctuations to guess the data being processed.

That reach is why data sovereignty matters for UK organisations. As US companies, the hyperscalers are potentially subject to US court orders that can compel them to exfiltrate overseas citizens’ data. 

The UK public sector is extremely exposed. In the 2023/2024 financial year, 95% of central and local public sector organisations spent budget on hyperscale cloud services, across more than 1,100 public sector bodies. The European Court of Justice has twice struck down data sharing agreements between the EU and the US – Schrems I and Schrems II – because Section 702 offers no equivalent protection to EU citizens.

The senators are not alone. A coalition of more than 20 civil liberties and accountability groups, led by Demand Progress and signed by the Center for Democracy & Technology, the American Civil Liberties Union and the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told congressional leaders the opinion must be public before any reauthorisation debate.

The dispute turns on a statutory transparency rule. Under US law, the director of national intelligence and the attorney general must complete a declassification review of significant FISA court opinions within 180 days. Senate intelligence committee chair Tom Cotton and vice-chair Mark Warner pressed for the opinion’s release in the spring, and Blanche said in July he would declassify it. The 13 September deadline passed in silence.

The senators wrote: “If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive, it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

title: Autumn Budget 2026: UK chancellor ties datacentre grid access to community tests
raw_text:
In his Autumn Budget, UK chancellor John Healey has made priority grid connections for datacentres conditional on strict tests around community investment, local jobs and water supplies.

This British “datacentre covenant” comes as Westminster takes in a datacentre backlash that has paused development across Scotland, and seen protests and petitions spring up across the UK.

Healey said the covenant would require operators to invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies before winning faster grid connections and, where necessary, permission to build on-site generation. 

He framed the need for datacentres around sovereignty, and argued that when the NHS uses artificial intelligence (AI) to treat patients, or the armed forces use it to keep the country safe, that data should stay in Britain. He cast the covenant as a new deal for datacentres, promising the grid connections operators need in exchange for the local consent they have struggled to win.

The move comes amid a ballooning datacentre pipeline that has grown to 173 projects and more than 14GW of capacity, driven by AI demand, and large sites in Scotland and the North East.

“I’m today launching a new British datacentre covenant with strict tests that datacentres must meet to invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies,” said Healey.

The covenant formed part of a wider AI package in the first Budget of Andy Burnham’s government, which added £500m for AI safety and security, £140m for the sovereign AI unit, and an AI Challenge Prize for public services. It also set aside £18m for advanced chip design led by Edinburgh University and £6m for the Glasgow Scottish Event Campus.

  • Data dive: Government 2030 datacentre capacity targets look shaky: We analyse why DSIT's 6GW AI-capable capacity target for 2030 is out of reach unless operators accelerate delivery.

It landed weeks after MSPs in Scotland rejected a Green call for a full moratorium, but voted to pause planning and consenting decisions on large datacentres until national guidance arrives by Christmas, with environmental impact assessments now required for any scheme of more than 50MW.

The vote followed a summer in which the SNP’s national council backed a moratorium and ministers intervened in individual schemes. Scotland’s committed pipeline has grown to 14 schemes and 2.4GW, the fastest growth of any UK region.

Opposition to datacentres has been evident in recent weeks. A petition against a datacentre at Little Bollington in Cheshire passed 1,000 signatures this week, and campaigners are urging rejection of a 700-acre solar and datacentre development in West Norfolk. The grid connection queue, rather than planning consent, remains the binding constraint on much of the pipeline, and Ireland already shows what happens when development outruns the grid.

For datacentre operators and the enterprise buyers that depend on them, the covenant offers a trade: commit to local benefits and win a faster route to power.

Whether those strict tests satisfy the communities now organising against individual schemes remains the open question.

title: Autumn Budget 2026: Chancellor sets aside funds for UK tech
raw_text:
Just over 30 minutes into his Autumn Budget speech, UK chancellor John Healey referenced the importance of artificial intelligence (AI) to the UK, and the route the government needs to take.

“Nowhere is the necessary role for the state clearer than in AI, to forge a British way, to seize opportunities and guard against the risks that is based on security,” he said.

Healey spoke about the UK’s role as a world leader in AI safety and security, which he announced is being backed by an extra £500m. This, said Healey, would be “based on sovereignty”, with what he described as a “first of its kind” Sovereign AI Unit that would protect UK interests by channeling government investment into strategic British AI firms.

As part of this investment in home-grown technology, Healey announced that these British strategic AI firms would be backed by £140m, “to ensure our most sensitive data stays under British control”.

“When the NHS uses AI to treat patients, we want that data here,” he said. “When our armed forces use AI to keep us safe, we want that data here.”

As part of this commitment, Healey announced a British datacentre covenant, which he said would mean datacentres would need to pass “strict tests”, covering investment in local communities, local job creation and the protection of local water supplies. In return, he promised that critical datacentres would get grid connections and, where necessary, be allowed to build on-site generation while they wait. 

His speech implies that the datacentre covenant will stipulate sovereignty and security as part of the criteria for new builds.

AI Challenge Prize

Healey also spoke about the AI Challenge Prize, which he said is there to ensure British people can benefit from the potential upsides of AI. This aims to support innovative uses for AI in public services.

There is also what he called the Union Learning Fund, created to back workers. “This is how Britain leads on AI: secure, safe and working for the British people,” said Healey.

Along with the tech funding boost, the Chancellor said he would be taking on board recommendations from the Women in Tech task force. “I’m also announcing a new scale-up programme to support female founders, and the British Business Bank will double its commitments to women-led businesses and funds to £200m,” he said.

Healey said the government would be reforming skilled worker visas and non-compete clauses in contracts, which he said means people who help build one successful company can move easily to the next. 

Commenting on the investments in AI, Louise Newbury-Smith, head of UK and Ireland at Zoom, said: “As the government sets out today’s Budget, AI remains one of the most powerful tools the UK has to drive long-term growth. The UK’s ambition to become an AI superpower will be won on adoption, and that must happen not just in boardrooms, but in town halls, high streets and small businesses in every region.”
 
While the Chancellor has set out his ambitions to support sovereign tech, there are plenty of barriers that put established US tech providers at a distinct advantage.

Mark Boost, CEO at sovereign cloud provider Civo, noted that public sector tech spending is often mainly focused on buying from abroad. “If public spending continues defaulting abroad, AI will be running on foreign providers’ platforms, with all of the value produced flowing overseas,” he said. “All of the government’s best-laid plans for its AI goals will go awry if its procurement bravery fails to match its rhetorical ambition.

“It is clear that John Healey wants this public spending to serve as a growth engine for every postcode in Britain,” said Boost. “Digital infrastructure is one of the best ways to achieve this. The UK already has homegrown providers building capacity across the country. It’s now time to back open, sovereign platforms across public services, and commit to buying from UK-owned and operated providers.”

title: Beyond power: How to avoid water as a constraint on AI growth
raw_text:
For several years, the race to build AI infrastructure has centred on one question – where will the power come from?  Today, across Europe and beyond, the next major constraint on AI growth is the resources required to remove the vast quantities of heat generated by high-density computing. 

As rack densities move beyond 100kW and AI deployments scale towards gigawatt-sized campuses, water availability is becoming a critical factor in determining where new capacity can be built, how quickly it can be deployed and whether it can expand over time.

In this environment, cooling is a strategic infrastructure decision.

AI’s hidden resource challenge: water

For many operators, water availability is increasingly important when evaluating future capacity. A site may have access to land and power, but if cooling depends on large volumes of evaporative water use, long-term growth plans can quickly run into practical limits.

While rack density is rising and global datacentre electricity demand is projected to more than double by 2030, drought, extreme heat and water uncertainty are becoming real constraints on where and how facilities are built and add pressure to already-strained infrastructure. 

Operators also now need to increasingly consider the availability of water. The question has shifted from how to cool a single rack to how the entire thermal system should be designed so cooling never becomes the constraint on growth.  

A facility may have access to sufficient power and land, for example, but limited water availability could affect how much computing capacity can ultimately be supported. Similarly, a cooling architecture designed around today’s workloads may become a limitation as rack densities increase.

Thermal management, therefore, needs to be considered alongside capacity planning, rather than after decisions around compute and site design have already been made.

Zero-water and higher-temperature cooling are expanding what’s possible

The industry's challenge is not to adopt a single new cooling technology. It is to integrate the entire thermal ecosystem. From direct-to-chip liquid cooling and coolant distribution units through to chillers and heat rejection systems, operators increasingly need architectures that optimise water, energy efficiency and computing performance simultaneously.  They need to consider an approach which focuses on treating these elements as a connected thermal strategy rather than individual infrastructure components.

Zero-water cooling is particularly significant because it changes the resource equation. Designs that eliminate evaporative heat rejection can remove dependence on a water-intensive cooling process and give operators greater flexibility when evaluating potential sites and planning future expansion. At the gigawatt scale, zero-water designs have modelled the potential to eliminate more than 45 million litres of cooling water consumption per day.  

That flexibility has implications beyond sustainability. If water availability no longer determines whether a site can support a particular cooling architecture, more locations can potentially become viable for datacentre development.

Similarly, higher condenser temperatures, up to 74°C, are expanding the role dry coolers can play in datacentre design. By allowing more heat to be rejected directly to ambient air, these approaches can reduce reliance on water-intensive cooling towers while also cutting noise levels by as much as 20dBA. Depending on the application, this can equate to a perceived noise reduction of up to 75%, resulting in sound levels comparable to a normal conversation or a quiet household appliance.

They can also reduce the amount of infrastructure dedicated to heat rejection, and give operators greater flexibility in site design and future expansion planning. Less water, less noise and a smaller cooling footprint open up sites near communities or in land- and water-constrained areas and can help facilities deploy and expand faster.

The business case goes beyond saving water

The value of zero-water cooling is therefore not simply the amount of water it can save. It is the capacity and flexibility that can be unlocked when water is no longer a fundamental constraint on cooling. Datacentres use significant energy beyond compute, with cooling accounting for an estimated 30% to 40% of total datacentre energy use.

Every resource used by cooling is a resource that cannot be used for compute, and every constraint that limits cooling can ultimately limit the amount of compute a facility can support.

Optimised thermal architectures can effectively return resources to the compute side of the facility. Modeled 1GW air-cooled architectures have demonstrated the potential to support up to 50 MW of additional AI capacity through thermal optimisation alone, and absorption-based designs that use on-site waste heat have shown potential for up to 97 MW of additional AI capacity.

There is another factor that is beginning to influence datacentre development – social licence to operate.

Across Europe, communities and regulators are paying closer attention to how datacentres consume local resources. Water use is increasingly part of that discussion. Reducing dependence on evaporative cooling does more than improve sustainability metrics. It can strengthen stakeholder confidence, simplify planning conversations and improve the long-term viability of future projects

Designing for growth from day one

As AI infrastructure continues to scale, thermal management will be a deciding factor in where and how new datacentre capacity gets built. The question is no longer simply whether a site has enough power to support AI. It is whether the site has the resources, infrastructure and cooling architecture needed to support that growth over time.

That means building thermal management into early decisions around site selection, capacity planning and infrastructure design, rather than treating cooling as a fixed requirement to solve after the workload is already set. Zero-water and higher-temperature cooling approaches can give operators more flexibility as rack densities increase, climate conditions change and resource constraints grow.

As the industry enters a period of unprecedented expansion, the next decade will require a broader question – can infrastructure be designed to grow without becoming constrained by the resources needed to cool it?

Organisations that answer that question early will gain greater flexibility in where they build, how quickly they scale and how effectively they navigate future resource constraints. In the AI era, cooling is no longer a support function, it is a strategic enabler of growth.

title: Austrian doctors to swap emails and phone calls for encrypted messages
raw_text:
Hospitals and clinics in Austria are gearing up to replace emails and phone calls with an end-to-end encrypted instant messaging service that promises to speed up communications between medical professionals and reduce the time it takes to make clinical decisions.

The country is conducting trials of a sovereign instant messenger service, based on open source technology, that will allow clinicians to send messages and securely share medical information.

The move follows plans by Germany to roll out its own encrypted messaging service, TI-Messenger, for healthcare, after trials showed that it saved clinicians time by freeing them from making repeated phone calls to speak with colleagues who are often too busy to answer the phone.

The catalyst for Austria to rethink how healthcare organisations communicate came in January 2025 when the government banned the use of faxes to exchange clinical information.

Alternatives to fax

Hospitals developed alternatives, such as encrypted email or encrypted file storage, to share medical data, but the profusion of different tools made it difficult for hospitals to communicate with each other.

Austria’s non-profit body ELGA GmbH, tasked with running the country’s electronic healthcare record system, began investigating alternatives to fax communications before the ban came into force.

In December 2024, it held a workshop on Matrix messenger, an open source encrypted messaging service, and adopted it as a standard a month later.

Matrix, which describes itself as an open protocol for decentralised secure communications, is coordinated by a non-profit community interest company, the Matrix.org Foundation.

Austria chose Matrix because it is decentralised, allowing every state or hospital to run their own server. The protocol allows end-to-end encryption – a requirement for patient data – and is already widely used in Germany and other parts of Europe.

The Matrix side project

One of the first implementations of Matrix in Austria began as a side project by two doctors in Salzburg, who shared a passion for open source software. They set up medSpeak in 2023 to offer a secure communications platform to other doctors in the region.

Phillipp Kurtz, co-founder and joint CEO of Famedly, a German technology company that is now involved in the development of Matrix in Austria, said the doctors were running a Matrix server from their surgery. “They had a little server and set it up themselves and ran all of their other hospitals and their other GPs in Salzburg on that server,” he added. He estimates that between 2,000 and 3,000 doctors have signed up to medSpeak.

That project expanded into a larger trial with the largest healthcare provider in Salzburg, Salzburger Landeskliniken (SALK), and a hospital in the state of Upper Austria, Klinikum Wels-Grieskirche.

The trial, which covered five hospitals, 7,100 staff, and was linked to the MedSpeak network, showed that encrypted messages could be shared successfully between doctors in different Austrian states.

Technical support was provided by Famedly, which designed the Matrix app for German healthcare organisations, and healthcare IT services company X-tention.

    Healthcare directory

    Kurtz told Computer Weekly that the pilot demonstrated the need to build a directory on top of Matrix, to allow medical staff to find each other on the messaging system.

    The project used a blueprint for a staff directory developed for TI-Messenger in Germany, and worked to the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) specification, a standard for electronically exchanging information.

    The trial improved the speed of communication between hospital doctors and GPs. Rather than phone or leave messages, GPs were able to message doctors in the hospital directly to ask questions about medication and care, after their patients were discharged from treatment.

    The latest proof of concept, which started in October 2026, has been organised by ELGA, which added Vienna and the federal state of Tyrol to the trial. It will test the ability of Matrix services hosted on different platforms to interoperate with each other.

    The proof of concept is supported by three technology suppliers – Famedly, Cloudfight and CompuGroup Medical – which are each running Matrix servers.

    Pragmatic approach

    Kurtz said he expected Austria to be able to deploy its messaging service quickly, as it takes a more pragmatic approach to technology than Germany. “The requirements for certification are way lower, so you don’t have to certify every single component separately,” he said.

    Austria also has an electronic ID system in place, which will make it quicker for doctors to sign up to an existing messaging service hub.

    Austrian health organisations can also opt to share Matrix servers, making the service cheaper to run.

    “My perception is that they want to have it rolled out, in 2028 at the latest, in the whole of Austria. They really, really want to ramp it up,” said Kurtz.

    One-stop shop

    Using a shared technology across the Austrian health service will allow clinicians to talk to their counterparts in other healthcare institutions more easily and quickly, said Kurtz.

    “You have one shared platform, one shared technology, and as long as you comply with that, you can talk to anyone in the system. So it’s really a one-stop shop for all your communication with other healthcare institutions,” he added.

    The service is expected to be particularly valuable when junior doctors working in a hospital need advice from a consultant or a senior doctor waiting at home on call.

    “The junior doctor doesn’t know what to do, so he just takes a photo of an ECG or X-ray or whatever and sends it via chat to the doctor on call, who can send a message back without having to come into the hospital,” said Kurtz.

    The service is also expected to find applications in nursing homes, making it easier for doctors to communicate with pharmacies when they prescribe medication to residents.

    Currently, the process takes multiple phone calls and follow-up faxes, which doctors are required to sign off manually.

    In future, Kurtz predicts that Austrian and German hospitals will federate their messaging services to allow doctors in both countries to collaborate.

    “Especially in winter, how many Germans go skiing in Austria and break a leg? There are always things to discuss between the German doctors and the Austrian doctors,” said Kurtz.

    Managing stakeholders

    Kurtz said the biggest challenge has been the need to manage a large number of stakeholders, which include federal states, hospitals, central and federal governments, and doctors using the homegrown medSpeak platform.

    “They all want to have a say in it, so bringing all the interests together and coming up with a joint standard … has been crazily complicated with all the stakeholders,” he added.

    Another challenge is that hospitals in Austria rely on shared inboxes, representing, for example, a ward where multiple people may be working. This format is not currently supported by Matrix.

    “Matrix just simply doesn’t have a good concept for this. This is something that’s missing and making implementation for these use cases extremely hard,” said Kurtz.

    The project is improving by using a group chat room that receives all the messages sent to doctors on the ward. The system uses a bot to discuss the request with several staff on the ward to find out which doctor should respond to the enquiry. The doctor can then reply to the message in a new private chat.

    Less talk, more action

    Matrix will become available to health providers in Austria from 2027, with a number of providers offering servers and messenger apps.

    Kurtz said that although medical professionals realise they need to have a system like Matrix, the challenge will be changing their behaviour so they don’t continue to use faxes or WhatsApp.

    “The most important leverage we have is the chief of medicine – if they are convinced and they tell their people to use just the Matrix-based solution, they will,” said Kurtz.

    Were he to do the project over again, Kurtz said he would be more pragmatic, by talking less with stakeholders and acting more.

    “Trial and error gets you to your goal a lot faster than trying to think through all the ways to use Matrix, which we have done in countless discussions, workshops and meetings. I would say, we just start with something basic and see what happens,” he said.

    Austria’s Matrix timeline

    • April 2024: First Matrix messenger service certified in Germany for healthcare.
    • December 2024: Workshop on Matrix Messenger held in Austria with ELGA GmbH, which is responsible for Austria’s electronic healthcare infrastructure.
    • January 2025: The Matrix protocol is adopted into Austrian health care standards.
    • January 2025: Austria bans use of fax machines for sending patient data.
    • March 2025: Federal government, states and social insurance agree on one joint Matrix solution.
    • August 2025: Famedly, a German Matrix app developer, is tasked with producing first draft for a national specification.
    • February 2026:  Implementation project launched with a number of technology suppliers.
    • July 2026: Architecture workshops with technology suppliers.
    • October 2026: Tests across Austrian states.
    • 2027: Beginning of national roll-out in healthcare.

title: Aera addresses decision-making using enterprise AI
raw_text:
Aera Technology used its AeraHUB 26 conference in New York to introduce and detail the mechanics driving six new services that work in agentic decision intelligence, designed to accelerate the methods and processes by which enterprises build, govern and scale automated decision-making.  

Aera said organisations running new-age agentic services today need the ability to capture business context, enforce policies, retain decision histories and continuously improve outcomes as autonomous agents make and execute choices. 

The capabilities it has built aim to connect decisions across the value chain, turn business challenges into repeatable decision automation, and capture and retain the knowledge, policies and outcomes behind every decision. According to Aera, these capabilities shift businesses to decision-centric enterprises, where decisions are continuously optimised and executed to drive measurable business outcomes.

Discussing the challenges in automating decision-making, Shariq Mansoor, co-founder and chief technology officer of Aera Technology, said: “A decision has options, trade-offs, rules and an outcome someone answers for, and in most companies it still lives in meetings and spreadsheets, and is forgotten the next day.”

This, he said, is the “what, why, when and where” behind the technology Aera has built.

“We have designed, tested and built one system where decisions are made, checked against the company’s policies, recorded with their reasoning, and learned from [it]. The language model is one part inside it, and we replace it as better ones arrive,” said Mansoor. 

The Aera team said realising greater value from AI requires fundamentally changing how businesses operate, starting with the decisions that drive operational performance – what to make, where to ship, when to buy, and how to meet customer demand. This means moving from data-driven decision-making to being decision-centric. It requires moving away from using data to inform or justify choices to engineering how decisions are made, executed and improved.

“The next unlock for enterprise performance is better decisions across the value chain,” said Fred Laluyaux, co-founder and CEO of Aera Technology. “AI is already making people more productive, but the bigger opportunity is transforming how businesses make and execute decisions. That is the shift to a decision-centric enterprise. With today’s innovations, we are making it dramatically easier to put that vision into practice.”

As AI takes on a greater role in enterprise decision-making, Laluyaux said: “Reasoning alone is not enough.”

Although an agent can perform a task, he said a decision has a plethora of options, trade-offs, policies and an outcome someone is accountable for.  

Building, governing and scaling decision intelligence  

Building on Aera’s foundation for agentic reasoning, the company is providing a skill-building capability. The idea is that users can start with a business challenge in plain language, prompt Aera to develop a plan, review and refine the proposed approach, approve it, and turn it into governed decision automation, often within a single working session.

Skills are created, refined and updated by talking to Aera. The company said this enables organisations to adapt and improve decisions continuously as business needs change.

Aera has also introduced Decision Ledger, which creates a persistent, traceable record of every decision, whether made in Aera or sent from another system through Aera’s application programming interface, capturing the business context, reasoning, policies evaluated, actions and outcomes behind each one.

Aera said it can spot decisions made in conversation and prompt a person to confirm them. By bringing structured and situational decisions into a common record, the company said it is able to preserve institutional knowledge, supports audit and review, and makes past decisions and their outcomes available to inform future decisions.  

The Policy Studio feature is designed to let organisations turn enterprise policies into rules that govern decisions as they are made. Teams upload a policy document or describe a rule in plain language, and Aera drafts the rules for a person to approve.

Rules can be tested against live decisions before enforcement. Once active, they apply consistently across relevant decision types and can block a decision, require approval or warn. The results of policy evaluations are captured in Decision Ledger, providing traceability and evidence of how decisions were governed.

“Our vision has always been to manage decisions as a digital asset: captured, governed and continuously improved,” said Mansoor. “These innovations automate that entire lifecycle, making it possible to capture every kind of decision, control the policies that govern them and enable the platform to learn from each one. And because the build itself is now automated, enterprises can automate far more decisions, far faster, and every skill becomes another digital asset they own.”

Other functions on offer include Agent Interoperability, to connect decision intelligence across the enterprise, and Dynamic UX, which enables users to create and adapt experiences using natural-language prompts.

The interoperability capabilities enable Aera to work with existing enterprise agents and tools, including Microsoft Copilot Studio, external agents through Agent2Agent, and external tools through Model Context Protocol.

Aera is also providing a feature called Command Center, which it said provides visibility into decision activity, performance and business impact enterprise-wide to help organisations monitor decisions, understand their outcomes and identify opportunities to improve performance as decision intelligence scales.

title: PHP2Shell: US updates Kev catalogue as exploits spread
raw_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (Cisa) has added the two so-called PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (Kev) catalogue after confirming live exploitation by unnamed threat actors.

The update addresses both CVE-2026-109618, a PHP memory corruption flaw, and CVE-2026-109619, a PHP stale internal request-state flaw.

First made public last week in a chaotic disclosure process, the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are considered critical due to the prevalence of the open source server-side scripting language across the World Wide Web. Collectively, they impact a huge number of organisations.

The addition of a vulnerability to the Kev list means civilian agencies of the US federal government must apply fixes to their systems by a specific date – in this case Thursday 29 October – and is a clear signal that the flaws in question are being exploited, meaning other organisations should pay attention even if they are not legally bound to do so.

“These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise,” the agency said.

Cisa said it was not known whether or not the PHP2Shell flaws have been implicated in any ransomware campaigns. Nor did it share details of any specific cyber incidents arising from them.

However, it emerged on Sunday 25 October that exploitation leading to remote code execution (RCE) had been detected against an Apache mod_php installation running version 8.4.26 of PHP in a sequestered honeypot environment.

Closed Door Security CEO William Wright said Cisa’s update had confirmed the fears that have been on many minds since PHP2Shell was made public last week.

“Before this, many security vendors had reported numerous attempts to target honeypots and servers using the vulnerabilities, though allegedly none had been successful in taking full advantage of the potential for RCE,” said Wright. 

“However, Cisa’s confirmation shows that the fear among experts and governments was not unjustified.

“Threat actors work rapidly and take advantage they can get, and the potential advantage here was massive, with the exploit effectively allowing attackers to control and modify any unpatched server exposed to the internet,” Wright told Computer Weekly via email.

He said that while major services have now been promptly patched, questions remain about what will happen to smaller sites and services – many of which may now not be maintained – and to instances in which PHP is hidden as part of a larger tech stack supporting other services.

Wright advised any organisations that have not yet started the process to review their systems as soon as possible to ensure they are not silently exposed to unpatched PHP deployments internally, or through third-party partners.

Time to exploit

According to CrowdStrike, full weaponisation of the PHP2Shell flaws likely took longer after disclosure because attackers would have needed to adapt the proof-of-concept exploit for the specific PHP version and application they wanted to target.

This presented a “meaningful barrier” to threat actors, the firm’s researchers said, because it meant they would have needed specific expertise on Docker containers, packages and other elements used by the would-be victim.

Meanwhile, as of 12.00pm UTC on 27 October, Infrawatch’s free PHP2Shell Tracker tool showed about 443,000 publicly visible hosts had been patched, an improvement of approximately 31,000 hosts in the previous 24 hours, representing around 20% of the total. In the UK, patches have been applied to 27.2% of visible hosts, and in the US, to 19.7%.

“Before this, many security vendors had reported numerous attempts to target honeypots and servers using the vulnerabilities, though allegedly none had been successful in taking full advantage of the potential for RCE,” said Wright. 

“However, Cisa’s confirmation shows that the fear among experts and governments was not unjustified.

“Threat actors work rapidly and take advantage they can get, and the potential advantage here was massive, with the exploit effectively allowing attackers to control and modify any unpatched server exposed to the internet,” Wright told Computer Weekly via email.

He said that while major services have now been promptly patched, questions remain about what will happen to smaller sites and services – many of which may now not be maintained – and to instances in which PHP is hidden as part of a larger tech stack supporting other services.

Wright advised any organisations that have not yet started the process to review their systems as soon as possible to ensure they are not silently exposed to unpatched PHP deployments internally, or through third-party partners.

Time to exploit

According to CrowdStrike, full weaponisation of the PHP2Shell flaws likely took longer after disclosure because attackers would have needed to adapt the proof-of-concept exploit for the specific PHP version and application they wanted to target.

This presented a “meaningful barrier” to threat actors, the firm’s researchers said, because it meant they would have needed specific expertise on Docker containers, packages and other elements used by the would-be victim.

Meanwhile, as of 12.00pm UTC on 27 October, Infrawatch’s free PHP2Shell Tracker tool showed about 443,000 publicly visible hosts had been patched, an improvement of approximately 31,000 hosts in the previous 24 hours, representing around 20% of the total. In the UK, patches have been applied to 27.2% of visible hosts, and in the US, to 19.7%.

title: OpenAI’s Altman: Only way out of patch apocalypse is through
raw_text:
At Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, Nevada, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has rallied the security community and called for cyber pros to keep focus, saying the only way out of the current tsunami of patches is through.

In conversation with Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk during the day two keynote, Altman aligned with Magouyrk that artificial intelligence (AI) is not necessarily creating the problem, but rather helping discover the myriad of security issues and flaws that have slowly developed over the past 20 to 30 years, and longer in some cases.

“I think the only way through this is to go and find all these issues and fix them,” said Altman. “In fact, I think we’ll need new ways to fix them. It’s maybe too hard to patch every bug one by one across the entire supply chain that we’re all dependent on. I think we’ll have to look at new kinds of services that are constantly monitoring traffic and not letting these things be exploited.

“But I find myself shocked at just how many vulnerabilities these AI systems are finding and what it’s going to take – just the incredible, Herculean effort that it’s going to take to get ahead of this.”

Asked what advice he would give to cyber pros at this point, Altman said: “If I could recommend only one thing to a company right now to do with AI in the very short term … it would be to really understand the security threat landscape from AI and mitigate against that.

“I do realise that this is probably somewhat annoying for me to say and you’re like, ‘Well, you’re creating the problem’,” he added.

Magouyrk said: “I’m glad that we are now able to discover [flaws] with AI rather than waiting for some unknown hacker to let us know about them.”

Cyber mesh

During the keynote session, Magouyrk added colour to new security initiatives trailed earlier at the event, with the formal announcement of the OpenAI-powered Oracle AI Security Mesh, designed to complement the existing Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Identity Assurance – a biometric human identity verification tool – and OCI Zero Trust Packet Routing – a network access policy enforcer.

Oracle proposes that this mesh service will enable its enterprise customers to strengthen protections across both applications and infrastructure whether they are running on-premise, in OCI, or in someone else’s cloud.

The combination of OpenAI’s latest frontier models with Oracle’s testing tools and contextual knowledge of customer systems will supposedly let users find and fix flaws by reasoning through application behaviour, investigating possible weaknesses, or assessing fixes.

Any changes or fixes applied will be human-approved with agents designed to operate with distinct identities, task-scope, and just-in-time permissions, and independent monitors will be on hand to detect and stop any agentic activity that ranges across approved boundaries.

Going deep with OpenAI

But Oracle’s tie-up with OpenAI does not stop with cyber security. The software supplier also today announced a collaboration with the AI giant to marry up its ChatGPT and Codex models to Oracle’s applications, data and cloud infrastructure to put AI to work across customer systems and operations.

An expanded product suite will bring this approach to life, said Oracle, by helping people to work across systems, build and deploy applications, and get on top of cyber issues. It described an “integrated foundation to build and run companies”.

“OpenAI is transforming how enterprises solve business problems, from chat, to coding, to analytics, to autonomous agents,” said Magouyrk.

“With this new product suite, we are uniting their transformative AI capabilities with Oracle applications, data and cloud infrastructure – technology that businesses around the world rely on to run their most critical operations.”

title: MWC Doha aims to position Middle East as global hub for AI and digital infrastructure
raw_text:
MWC Doha, which returns to Qatar for its second edition on 8-10 November, aims to establish the Middle East as a central player in global discussions around connectivity, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure, according to Jawad Abbassi, head of MENA at the GSMA.

While MWC has traditionally been associated with Barcelona and Shanghai, Abbassi said Doha offers a strategic location from which to connect markets across Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Europe, putting more than five billion people within reach.

“MWC Doha delivers a full-scale MWC experience, on par with Barcelona and Shanghai,” he said.

The event also provides a platform for governments to connect national digital strategies with private sector investment. Qatar National Vision 2030 and Saudi Vision 2030, alongside similar programmes across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), are driving investment in technology, infrastructure and economic diversification.

“MWC Doha’s role is to be that meeting point for the leaders and decision-makers that deliver those visions, and gives the Middle East and North Africa its own home within the GSMA’s global MWC series,” Abbassi said.

This year’s event coincides with the International Telecommunication Union’s (ITU) Plenipotentiary Conference (PP-26), bringing digital policymakers from more than 190 ITU member states to Doha alongside industry leaders and technology innovators. The GSMA sees the combination as an opportunity to bring policy discussions and industry priorities closer together.

From 5G roll-out to enterprise value

Across the Middle East, telecoms markets are moving beyond the initial deployment of 5G towards more advanced networks and new commercial opportunities. Abbassi identified the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait as among the world’s most advanced 5G markets, with operators progressing towards 5G Standalone, 5G-Advanced and reduced-capability technologies.

The next phase will depend on how effectively businesses translate connectivity investments into measurable economic outcomes. GSMA research projects that enterprise spending on digital transformation across MENA will average 9.8% of revenues between 2025 and 2030. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE are among the world’s top seven digital transformation spenders, according to Abbassi.

However, expanding network coverage alone will not be sufficient to realise the region’s digital ambitions. Although 96% of the MENA population lived within mobile broadband coverage, only 49% were using mobile internet by the end of 2023, he said. The difference highlights what the industry calls the mobile internet usage gap: people who live within coverage areas but do not use mobile internet services.

Closing that gap will require greater affordability, digital skills and locally relevant content, Abbassi said. Doing so could extend the benefits of connectivity to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), healthcare, education and underserved communities.

Telecoms operators take on a broader role in AI

As governments and businesses invest in AI, cloud computing and datacentres, telecoms operators are increasingly positioning themselves as infrastructure providers beyond traditional connectivity.

AI services require access to data, cloud capacity, edge infrastructure and reliable networks. Operators are therefore investing in the infrastructure needed to support increasingly data-intensive workloads, while also applying AI to their own network operations.

Abbassi pointed to du’s datacentre partnership with Microsoft and e&’s agreements with Huawei, Ericsson, Nokia and Intel to apply AI across its mobile networks as examples of how regional operators are expanding their role in the technology ecosystem.

Network application programming interfaces (APIs) represent another opportunity. Through the GSMA’s Open Gateway initiative, operators can expose standardised network capabilities to developers, making it easier to build services that use telecoms infrastructure without negotiating separate arrangements in every market.

For developers and enterprise technology teams, the initiative could simplify access to network capabilities and create opportunities for services that depend on connectivity, security and network intelligence. The wider challenge will be turning infrastructure investment into scalable services and business models that deliver value beyond the telecoms sector.

Digital sovereignty and global partnerships

The region’s ambitions to develop sovereign AI capabilities and strengthen control over critical digital infrastructure are also reshaping technology investment.

Governments are seeking greater control over strategic assets, including data, computing capacity and semiconductor supply chains, while continuing to rely on international technology partners.

Abbassi explained that these objectives need not conflict. “Global collaboration has been a key driver of progress in the mobile and digital technology sectors, and the GSMA advocates for open markets and policies that support cross-border cooperation alongside each country’s own digital ambitions,” he said.

He cited Qatar and the UAE joining Pax Silica, a US-aligned initiative focused on semiconductor and AI supply chains, alongside their investments in domestic AI infrastructure.

Qatar Investment Authority’s $2bn expansion of its venture capital programme, aimed at attracting global funds and AI startups to Doha, is another example of the country’s efforts to combine sovereign investment with international participation.

For technology leaders, the balance between sovereignty and collaboration will have implications for cloud strategy, infrastructure sourcing, data governance and access to advanced AI capabilities.

Abbassi said global partnerships would remain critical to scaling AI responsibly, with open standards and predictable regulatory environments helping countries pursue national priorities while maintaining international cooperation.

AI, intelligent economies and connected infrastructure

MWC26 Doha’s programme is organised around three themes: AI in Action, Intelligent Economies and Connected Infrastructure.

AI in Action will examine how telecoms companies are turning embedded intelligence into practical outcomes. Intelligent Economies will focus on the policies and partnerships needed to build competitive and inclusive digital economies. Connected Infrastructure will explore how next-generation networks can deliver performance, resilience and security at scale.

Dedicated summits will cover sovereign AI and national digital strategy, intelligent datacentres, agentic AI, open telecoms AI, future networks, and satellite and non-terrestrial networks (NTNs).

The agenda reflects the increasingly interconnected nature of the region’s digital transformation priorities. AI adoption depends on computing infrastructure and connectivity, while the commercial success of those investments relies on enterprise demand, regulatory frameworks and access to skills and capital.

Turning regional ambition into partnerships

For the GSMA, success at MWC26 Doha will depend on building on the inaugural event and demonstrating sustained international interest in the region’s technology ambitions.

Abbassi identified two priorities: showcasing global interest in MENA’s digital future, and demonstrating why the region is positioned to help shape the future of connectivity, AI and digital infrastructure. For the wider technology ecosystem, he said the event should serve as a catalyst for collaboration, connecting policy priorities with industry investment and giving regional innovation greater international visibility.

“MWC Doha will continue to act as a meeting point and productivity catalyst where conversations become partnerships, policy priorities align with industry investment, and regional innovation gets showcased to a global audience,” Abbassi added.

title: Azure licensing lock-in limits choice
raw_text:
A survey of 410 software and cloud decision-makers in US businesses has found that organisations are putting off investment due to Microsoft software licensing costs.

Respondents reported finding that costs are higher when using a cloud provider other than Microsoft Azure to host Microsoft software. According to the Coalition for Fair Software Licensing, this demonstrates that customers are being steered to Azure through financial penalty rather than merit, and workloads are being locked out of the cloud.

Over half of affected businesses (56%) have increased prices to cover the cost. The same number have also cut other spending, while 33% have slowed hiring.

The survey also reported that 83% claimed Microsoft’s licensing rules have a meaningful impact on their choice of cloud provider. In fact, 18% said they have never considered a competing provider, while 61% of organisations that did look at alternatives still selected Azure to avoid fees.

Ryan Triplette, executive director of the Coalition for Fair Software Licensing, said: “Microsoft’s customers are telling us the system is broken. Businesses are being steered to Azure by financial penalties rather than by merit. They are passing the costs on to their own customers and delaying [investment in] the AI [artificial intelligence] tools they need to compete. Some are choosing not to migrate to the cloud at all, rather than incur the costs associated with Microsoft’s licences to do so.”

Triplette said the survey showed that the closer a decision-maker is to Microsoft’s licensing practices, the more urgently they want regulators to step in. She urged regulators to take note: “What happens next matters to every American business, and every consumer paying more because of Microsoft’s anti-competitive licensing practices.” 

Under the UK’s Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, a company designated as having strategic market status (SMS) has substantial and entrenched market power and a position of strategic significance in respect of a digital activity.

In the UK, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has been investigating whether Microsoft should be designated with SMS with regard to its business software, which includes its Office productivity suite, Windows and SQL Server.

Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA, said: “Business software and cloud services underpin workplaces across the UK, from small firms to vital public services. The evidence shows Microsoft has a long-standing and significant presence in the UK’s business software market.

“Organisations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives.

“We’re now consulting on whether to designate Microsoft with strategic market status. If we do, our focus would be on promoting competition and giving businesses greater freedom to choose and combine products in business software.”

Microsoft has also been battling with European regulators.

In 2023, the European Commission began a formal investigation to assess whether Microsoft may have breached European Union competition rules by tying or bundling its communication and collaboration product Teams to its popular suites for businesses Office 365 and Microsoft 365.

This led to changes to Microsoft licensing across the European Economic Area and Switzerland, where the company agreed to unbundle Teams from its Office suite.

title: TechEd 2026: SAP fronts tabular data model in space as it bids to make autonomous enterprise real
raw_text:
At SAP TechEd 2025 in Berlin, Philipp Herzig, chief technology officer of SAP, finished the opening keynote with a flourish in space. The supplier’s tabular data foundation model, RPT-2, is being deployed, with technology from HPE, aboard the International Space Station. RPT-1 [pronounced “rapid one”] was announced at TechEd last year. It functions like a large language model [LLM] that will predict the next word in a sentence, but for structured data, according to SAP. It is used to make predictions for business scenarios, such as delivery delays or payment risk.

“If we can run maintenance predictions in one of the most unforgiving environments, think what this means for our operations here on Earth,” said Herzig. “That’s AI [artificial intelligence] proven under pressure.”

In a blog post, Brenda Brown, the supplier’s chief marketing officer for SAP Business AI Platform and Joule, said: “SAP [has] announced the planned deployment of SAP-RPT, our tabular AI foundation model, on HPE Spaceborne Computer-2 aboard the International Space Station (ISS), one of the most significant edge compute validations of an enterprise AI model to date.”

She further said the model “makes predictions directly from structured data – even with some data missing – and without requiring the usual model training or fine-tuning. Running directly onboard the ISS on HPE Spaceborne Computer-2, it supports anomaly triage in real-time telemetry data, predicts issues before failures escalate, reconstructs missing sensor values based on historical data, and generates explainable mission-health reports for astronauts and ground teams.”

In a press statement, Herzig added: “The same trusted SAP-RPT model that powers global supply chains also can work in space.

“SAP’s deep-rooted, proven expertise has led to the International Space Station’s use of our tabular foundation model to predict potential mission-critical failures in orbit,” he said. “With SAP RPT and TabPFN from [SAP acquisition] Prior Labs, we bring the unique capabilities of tabular AI into the enterprise and across every frontier.”

The broad theme of TechEd is to put some flesh on the bones of the “autonomous enterprise” vision adumbrated at this year’s Sapphire conferences in Florida and Madrid.

Evolution

Florian Kunzke, SAP’s global director of artificial intelligence strategy, said in a pre-conference press briefing with international press: “We will see an evolution of our strategy so far, moving from the slides in our announcements at Sapphire into the productive environments of our customers, which is the hardest thing to do.”

The supplier is announcing enhancements to its Joule Studio and Joule Work technologies, and its Business AI Platform, including the tabular foundation model on board the space station. The supplier describes Joule Work as “a foundational capability within SAP’s AI suite that orchestrates complex business workflows, automates cross-functional tasks, and manages end-to-end operational processes autonomously across enterprise applications”.

SAP is also putting forward new tools to build AI agents and endeavouring to provide a “richer data and business context for those agents to reason with, and strengthened governance controls to run them responsibly across the enterprise”.

Herzig said, in the main statement for the event: “SAP TechEd has always been where builders shape what comes next,” he said, adding that this was the 30th event of its kind. “This year, we are showing how we are moving from AI learning your business to running it. Joule Work is where you put your intent and get work done, in one experience across the entire SAP landscape and beyond. That is the shift we are delivering at scale.

“Everything underneath runs on SAP Business AI Platform, delivering faster time to value, business understanding, higher accuracy, enterprise-readiness that is secure, governed and compliant, and a unique context layer built on over 50 years of process and industry expertise, encoded into every agent action.”

At last week’s SAP AI Tour event in Birmingham, Manos Raptopoulos, global president of customer success, said in the keynote session: “AI means technology is now back in the boardroom, but is it delivering business value? When LLMs can’t do Arithmetic, 90% accuracy is not good enough for businesses.”

He argued that grounding SAP’s AI technology Joule in a “context layer” made possible by customers’ use of the supplier’s enterprise resource planning over many years “reduces hallucinations by 89%”, adding that specific business knowledge, semantic richness and governance are what AI needs to deliver business value for SAP customers.

In an interview with Computer Weekly, Raptopoulos said that when it comes to getting business value from AI, “the first layer is the intelligence layer, which is your generative AI model, LLM, call it whatever. There is another layer, which is the context layer, and context here is twofold. One is the context of the system – when it comes at least to our own system, it’s the Knowedge Graph, as we call it, or the ontology, as some other people call it, but it’s also the context of the company, which we call company memory in terms of, “So how do we do things around here?”

“To get to what we call the autonomous enterprise, every customer is at a point A, and they have to go to point B,” he said. “There are certain customers that are more advanced on that journey, and every customer is somehow unique, but they are very much aware of that journey, of that transformation that they need to do.”

At TechEd, the supplier is announcing capabilities for Joule Work, said to help make AI agents be more effective at handling complex business processes via open protocols including Agent2Agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP). 

It talks about “agentic thinking capabilities that plan and orchestrate the steps assistants and agents need to reliably complete complex, multi-step business workflows across SAP landscapes”.

The supplier is also trumpeting master data management capabilities provided by recent acquisition Reltio and data lake capabilities proffered by another recent acquisition, Dremio. That is said to have native support for Apache Iceberg and Apache Polaris, plus a high-performance, federated query engine that will enable unified data access without moving or copying the data. 

It is also announcing an expansion of its relationship with Databricks, whose CEO, Ali Ghodsi, had a message for the conference reaffirming its work with SAP.
